sk: द्वा सुपर्णा सयुजा सखाया समानं वृक्षं परिषस्वजाते तयोरन्यः पिप्पलं स्वाद्वत्त्यनश्नन्नन्यो अभिचाकशीति ||
ro: dvā · suparṇā · sayujā · sakhāyā · samānaṁ · vṛkṣaṁ · pariṣasvajāte · tayoḥ · anyaḥ · pippalaṁ · svādu · atti · anaśnan · anyaḥ · abhicākaśīti ||
hi: दो (द्वा) सुपर्ण (beautiful-winged birds / सुन्दर पंखों वाले पक्षी), सयुजा (inseparably united / सदा संयुक्त), सखाया (friends / companions / सखा) — समान वृक्ष (the same tree / एक ही वृक्ष) को परिषस्वजाते (have embraced / आलिंगन किए हुए हैं)। उन दोनों में से एक (अन्यः) पिप्पल (the fruit / फल) को स्वादु अत्ति (eats with relish / स्वाद ले-लेकर खाता है); दूसरा (अन्यः) अनश्नन् (not eating / बिना खाए) अभिचाकशीति (simply looks on / केवल देखता रहता है)।
en: Two birds (dvā suparṇā), inseparably united (sayujā), companions (sakhāyā), have embraced (pariṣasvajāte) the same tree (samānaṁ vṛkṣam). Of the two, one (anyaḥ) eats the sweet fruit (pippalaṁ svādu atti); the other (anyaḥ), not eating (anaśnan), simply looks on (abhicākaśīti).

ws.h: सुन्दर पंखों वाले पक्षी / beautiful-winged birds
ws.e: beautiful-winged — su (beautiful/good) + parṇa (wing/feather); poetic for 'birds'; the dual form indicates exactly two birds
inseparably united — sa (together) + yuj (joined); the two birds are never apart — they are eternally on the same tree; the jīva and Brahman are never truly separated
friends / companions — from sakhi (friend); the relationship is intimate, not hierarchical; the two birds are 'friends,' not master-servant
the fruit — pippala = the berry of the sacred fig tree (ficus religiosa / pīpal); symbolises the 'fruits' of karma — the results of action, both sweet and bitter

ws.h: स्वाद से खाता है / eats with relish
ws.e: eats with relish — svādu (sweet/delicious) + atti (eats); the jīva-bird 'eats' the fruits of karma with attachment and pleasure/pain

ws.h: केवल देखता है / simply looks on / witnesses
ws.e: simply looks on / gazes — intensive (frequentative) form of √cakṣ (to see); the witnessing bird watches intently but does not participate; pure awareness without involvement

gr: The two birds — the Upanishads' most famous parable: this is one of the most celebrated mantras in all Upanishadic literature, and one of the oldest surviving parables in Indian philosophy. The two birds: (1) The eating bird (jīva/individual self) — eats the fruit of the pīpal tree, experiencing pleasure and pain, joy and sorrow. This bird is the individual soul engaged with the world, reaping the fruits of karma. (2) The watching bird (ātman/Brahman/witness) — sits on the same tree, does not eat, simply watches. This bird is the supreme Self — pure awareness, the eternal witness (sākṣin) who is never affected by anything. samānaṁ vṛkṣam — 'the same tree': the tree is the body (or saṁsāra/the world). Both birds sit on the SAME tree — the jīva and Brahman share the same body, the same life, the same reality. They are 'inseparably united' (sayujā) and 'friends' (sakhāyā). The critical contrast: one eats (atti), the other watches (abhicākaśīti). One is involved, the other is detached. One suffers and enjoys, the other is eternally at peace. abhicākaśīti: the intensive/frequentative form of √cakṣ (to see) — not just 'sees' but 'intensely watches' / 'continuously gazes.' The witness doesn't glance casually — it watches with absolute, unwavering attention. Yet it never acts.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.1.1 — This mantra is virtually identical to Ṛg Veda 1.164.20 — one of the most ancient verses in the Vedic corpus, composed by the seer Dīrghatamas. The Śvetāśvatara (4.6) also reproduces it nearly verbatim. The parable is thus pan-Vedic — it spans from the earliest Ṛg Vedic hymns through the classical Upanishads. Shankara identifies: eating bird = jīva (individual self bound by avidyā); watching bird = Paramātmā (the supreme Self / Brahman / witness-consciousness). Ramanuja identifies: eating bird = jīva (the individual soul); watching bird = Nārāyaṇa (God as antaryāmī / inner controller). The tree (vṛkṣa) is variously interpreted as: the body, the world of saṁsāra, the field of karma, or the Vedic tree of life (aśvattha). The pippala (fruit) = the results of karma — both pleasant and unpleasant.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — दो पक्षी = (1) जीवात्मा — अज्ञान-वश कर्मफल (fruits of karma) खाता है — सुख-दुःख भोगता है। (2) परमात्मा / साक्षी-चैतन्य (witness-consciousness) — अनश्नन् (non-eating) — कर्मफल से अस्पृष्ट (untouched)। 'सयुजा सखाया' = दोनों सदा एक साथ — किन्तु एक (जीव) अज्ञान से ग्रस्त, दूसरा (ब्रह्म) सदा मुक्त।
advaita.en: Shankara says two birds = (1) the jīvātmā — eats the fruits of karma due to ignorance — experiences pleasure and pain. (2) Paramātmā / witness-consciousness — anaśnan (not eating) — untouched by karma-fruit. 'Sayujā sakhāyā' = both always together — but one (jīva) is bound by ignorance, the other (Brahman) is ever free.
advaita.ins: You are two birds sitting on one tree. One bird is you-as-you-think-you-are — eating the fruits of life, sometimes sweet, sometimes bitter, always wanting more. The other bird is you-as-you-really-are — the witness, the one who simply watches, untouched, at peace. The tragedy is that the eating bird has forgotten the watching bird. The liberation is remembering.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — दो पक्षी = (1) जीवात्मा — कर्मफल भोगने वाला — भगवान् से भिन्न (distinct) किन्तु अभिन्न (inseparable)। (2) भगवान् / अन्तर्यामी (inner controller) — अनश्नन् — कर्मफल नहीं भोगता — जीव का मार्गदर्शक (guide) और सखा (friend)। 'सखाया' = भगवान् जीव के सखा (friend/companion) हैं — स्वामी-भृत्य नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says two birds = (1) the jīvātmā — the enjoyer of karma-fruits — distinct from God but inseparable. (2) God / antaryāmī (inner controller) — anaśnan — does not enjoy karma-fruits — the guide and friend of the jīva. 'Sakhāyā' = God is the jīva's friend/companion — not master-servant.
vishisht.ins: Two birds, one tree. You're one bird — eating the fruits of your life, tasting sweetness and bitterness. God is the other bird — your companion, your friend, sitting right next to you, watching. He doesn't eat your karma. He watches, guides, loves. He's been with you since the beginning — on every tree, in every life.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — दो पक्षी = (1) मनोमय पुरुष (mental being) — संसार-वृक्ष (tree of world-existence) पर कर्मफल भोगता है। (2) अन्तरात्मा / psychic being — शुद्ध चेतना (pure consciousness) — साक्षी (witness) — अभिचाकशीति = 'intensely gazes' = चेतना सदा जागरूक (ever-aware)। दोनों एक ही अस्तित्व (existence) के दो पक्ष (aspects)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says two birds = (1) the mental being — enjoys the fruits on the tree of world-existence. (2) the inner Self / psychic being — pure consciousness — the witness — abhicākaśīti = 'intensely gazes' = consciousness ever-aware. Both are two aspects of one existence.
aurobindo.ins: Two aspects of you sit on the tree of your life. One eats — tasting every experience, sweet and bitter, always involved. The other watches — intensely aware, never eating, never losing itself. The eating is necessary — it's how consciousness explores the world. But the watching is what you fundamentally are.

dp.q: 🔍 The two birds — origin, meaning, and impact
dp.a: The two-birds parable is one of the most ancient, most famous, and most widely quoted images in Indian philosophy: Origin: this mantra first appears in the Ṛg Veda (1.164.20), composed by the seer Dīrghatamas — making it one of the oldest philosophical verses in human history (possibly 1500-1200 BCE). The Muṇḍaka reproduces it nearly verbatim. The Śvetāśvatara (4.6) also quotes it. The mapping: (1) Tree (vṛkṣa) = the body, or the world of saṁsāra, or the field of karma. It is the shared ground of experience — both birds sit on the SAME tree. (2) Eating bird = the jīva (individual self) — engaged with the world, experiencing pleasure and pain, eating the sweet and bitter fruits of karma. This bird is restless — always seeking the next fruit. (3) Watching bird = the ātman/Brahman/witness (sākṣin) — pure awareness, unmoving, uninvolved, simply gazing. This bird is at perfect peace — it has never eaten, never desired, never suffered. (4) Inseparably united (sayujā) = the two are never apart. Even in the deepest ignorance, Brahman is right beside the jīva — on the same tree, as a friend. The message: you are BOTH birds. You experience life (eating bird), but your true nature is the witness (watching bird). Liberation is not going to a new tree — it is seeing the bird you've always been.

dp.q: 🔍 'Abhicākaśīti' — the witness who intensely gazes
dp.a: The verb 'abhicākaśīti' deserves special attention — it reveals the nature of the witnessing Self: Grammar: abhicākaśīti is the intensive/frequentative form (yaṅ-luk) of √cakṣ (to see/perceive). The intensive form indicates repeated, intense, or continuous action. So it doesn't mean merely 'sees' but 'gazes intently' or 'watches continuously.' What this reveals about the witness: (1) The witness is not passive — it watches with intense attention. It sees everything — every fruit eaten, every pleasure, every pain — with perfect clarity. (2) The witness is not indifferent — the intensive form suggests deep, sustained awareness, not casual observation. The Self doesn't 'glance' at the world; it gazes. (3) The witness is not acting — despite watching intently, it does NOT eat. It has complete awareness without any involvement. Awareness without attachment. The practical significance for meditation: to find the 'watching bird,' don't try to stop awareness — instead, find the part of you that is already watching. You are already the witness in every moment — behind every thought, behind every emotion, behind every perception, there is something that simply watches. That is the second bird. That is you.

sk: समाने वृक्षे पुरुषो निमग्नोऽनीशया शोचति मुह्यमानः जुष्टं यदा पश्यत्यन्यमीशमस्य महिमानमिति वीतशोकः ||
ro: samāne · vṛkṣe · puruṣaḥ · nimagnaḥ · anīśayā · śocati · muhyamānaḥ · juṣṭaṁ · yadā · paśyati · anyam · īśam · asya · mahimānam · iti · vīta-śokaḥ ||
hi: समान वृक्ष (the same tree) पर पुरुष (the person / जीव) निमग्न (immersed / डूबा हुआ) है — अनीशया (due to helplessness / अशक्ति / lordlessness) शोचति (grieves / शोक करता है), मुह्यमान (deluded / मोहित) होता है। जब (यदा) वह जुष्टम् (the adored / worshipped) अन्यम् ईशम् (the other, the Lord / दूसरे पक्षी — ईश्वर) को पश्यति (sees / देखता है) — और अस्य महिमानम् (His glory) [जानता है] — तब (इति) वीतशोक (free from sorrow / शोक-रहित) हो जाता है।
en: On the same tree (samāne vṛkṣe), the person (puruṣa), immersed (nimagnaḥ), grieves (śocati) due to helplessness (anīśayā), deluded (muhyamānaḥ). But when (yadā) he sees (paśyati) the other (anyam), the Lord (īśam), the adored one (juṣṭam), and [realises] His glory (asya mahimānam) — then he becomes free from sorrow (vīta-śokaḥ).

ws.e: immersed / drowned — ni + √majj (to sink/drown); the jīva is 'drowned' in the world of saṁsāra — overwhelmed by experience, unable to surface

ws.h: अशक्ति से / अनीश्वरत्व से / due to helplessness
ws.e: due to helplessness / lordlessness — an + īśa (lord/master) + instrumental; the jīva grieves because it feels powerless — it has forgotten its connection to the Lord; it thinks it is alone and helpless
being deluded — present participle of √muh (to be bewildered/confused); the jīva is actively, continuously being deluded — delusion is an ongoing process, not a fixed state
the adored one — from √juṣ (to be pleased with/enjoy); the Lord is 'juṣṭa' — worthy of worship, the one in whom delight is found
free from sorrow — vīta (gone/departed) + śoka (sorrow/grief); sorrow has 'departed' — not suppressed but genuinely gone; the natural state of one who sees the Lord

gr: From grief to freedom — the turning point: this mantra is the emotional heart of the two-birds parable. The first mantra described the situation; this mantra describes the transformation. The jīva's condition: nimagnaḥ (immersed/drowned), anīśayā (helpless), śocati (grieves), muhyamānaḥ (deluded). Four words painting the picture of the individual soul's suffering — drowning in the world, feeling powerless, grieving, and confused. The turning point: 'yadā paśyati' — 'when he sees.' The moment of liberation is a seeing — the jīva turns and sees the other bird, the Lord (īśam), the watching witness who has been there all along. What causes the seeing? The mantra doesn't say the jīva earns it or deserves it — it simply says 'yadā' (when). The moment of recognition is not a product of effort alone but a grace-filled turning. vīta-śokaḥ — 'free from sorrow': the result is immediate. The moment the jīva sees the Lord, sorrow departs (vīta). Not gradually reduced, not managed — gone. Because sorrow was caused by 'anīśayā' (lordlessness/helplessness), and seeing the Lord is the direct remedy.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.1.2 — This mantra continues the two-birds parable from 3.1.1 but shifts from description to drama — the jīva's grief and its resolution. The Śvetāśvatara (4.7) has a closely parallel verse. The word 'anīśayā' is crucial and contested: Shankara reads it as 'due to not being the Lord (an-īśa)' = the jīva grieves because it mistakenly thinks it is a limited, powerless individual rather than recognising its identity with Brahman. Ramanuja reads it as 'due to being without the Lord (an-īśa)' = the jīva grieves because it has lost connection with the Lord; the remedy is to see the Lord (anyam īśam paśyati). The word 'juṣṭam' (adored) is particularly significant for Ramanuja — it describes the Lord as the one who is delighted in (by the liberated souls), reinforcing the bhakti dimension. The Kaṭha (1.2.22) uses a similar phrase: 'tam akratuḥ paśyati vīta-śokaḥ' — 'He sees that Self through the grace of the Creator, and becomes free from sorrow.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'अनीशया' = अज्ञान-वश जीव अपने को अनीश (powerless / limited) मानता है — इसी से शोचति (grieves)। 'अन्यम् ईशम् पश्यति' = जब जीव दूसरे पक्षी (परमात्मा / साक्षी / Brahman) को देखता है — अर्थात् अपनी ब्रह्म-स्वरूपता (Brahman-nature) को पहचानता है — तब 'वीतशोकः' = शोक-मुक्त। 'अन्यम्' = अन्य = वस्तुतः अन्य नहीं — वही अपना आत्मा।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'anīśayā' = due to ignorance, the jīva considers itself powerless/limited — hence it grieves. 'Anyam īśam paśyati' = when the jīva sees the other bird (Paramātmā / witness / Brahman) — i.e., recognises its own Brahman-nature — then 'vīta-śokaḥ' = free from sorrow. 'Anyam' = 'the other' = actually not other but one's own Self.
advaita.ins: You sit on the tree, drowning in experience, eating fruit after fruit, grieving because you feel powerless. Then one day you look up — and see the other bird. The one who's been watching all along. And in that moment you realise: that bird is you. The real you. And sorrow dissolves — because helplessness was only a case of mistaken identity.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'अनीशया' = जीव भगवान् से विच्छिन्न (disconnected) मानता है — इसलिए शोक। 'अन्यम् ईशम् पश्यति' = जब जीव भगवान् (the Lord) — जो सदा उसके साथ (सयुजा, सखाया) हैं — को देखता है, उनका महिमा (glory) जानता है — तब शोक-मुक्त। भगवद्-दर्शन (vision of God) = शोक-निवृत्ति (end of sorrow)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'anīśayā' = the jīva thinks it is disconnected from God — hence sorrow. 'Anyam īśam paśyati' = when the jīva sees God (the Lord) — who has always been with it (sayujā, sakhāyā) — and knows His glory — then it becomes sorrow-free. Vision of God = end of sorrow.
vishisht.ins: You've been sitting on the tree, feeling alone, overwhelmed, helpless. But look — right next to you sits your oldest friend, the Lord. He's been there through every life, every sorrow, every birth. When you finally turn and see Him — really see Him — sorrow ends. Not because the world changes, but because you see who's been beside you all along.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'निमग्नः' = मनोमय पुरुष (mental being) संसार-अनुभव (world-experience) में डूबा। 'अनीशया' = अहंकार (ego) के कारण — चेतना अपने को सीमित मानती है। 'ईशम् पश्यति' = जब व्यक्ति अन्तरात्मा (psychic being / inner Self) को देखता है — चेतना अपने विश्वव्यापी (universal) स्वरूप को पहचानती है — शोक गिर जाता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'nimagnaḥ' = the mental being is drowned in world-experience. 'Anīśayā' = due to the ego — consciousness considers itself limited. 'Īśam paśyati' = when one sees the inner Self (psychic being) — consciousness recognises its universal nature — sorrow falls away.
aurobindo.ins: You're drowning in your own experience — eating every fruit, overwhelmed by every sensation. You feel helpless because the ego tells you you're small, separate, alone. Then you see the other bird — the consciousness that was watching all along, the Self that was never drowning. And the grief that seemed so absolute simply falls away. It was never yours. It was the ego's.

dp.q: 🔍 'Anīśayā' — the root cause of grief
dp.a: The word 'anīśayā' identifies the root cause of the jīva's grief: Etymology: an-īśa = 'without lordship' / 'not being the lord' / 'helplessness.' Two readings: (1) Advaita: 'anīśayā' = because the jīva thinks it is NOT the Lord (an-īśa) — i.e., it has forgotten its identity with Brahman. The grief comes from mistaken identity — thinking 'I am a limited, powerless individual' when in fact 'I am Brahman.' The remedy: recognise your identity with the watching bird. (2) Viśiṣṭādvaita: 'anīśayā' = because the jīva is WITHOUT the Lord (an-īśa) — i.e., it has lost its connection with God. The grief comes from separation — feeling alone when God is actually right beside you (sayujā, sakhāyā). The remedy: turn and see the Lord (anyam īśam paśyati). Both readings agree: (a) the root cause of sorrow is a failure of seeing — not seeing the Lord/Self who is always present. (b) The remedy is also a seeing — 'yadā paśyati' (when he sees). (c) The result is immediate — 'vīta-śokaḥ' (sorrow departs). The practical implication: grief is not caused by external circumstances but by an internal failure of vision. The Lord is always right beside you (on the same tree). Your sorrow comes not from the world but from not seeing the companion who shares your tree.

dp.q: 🔍 The moment of recognition — 'yadā paśyati' (when he sees)
dp.a: The phrase 'yadā paśyati' ('when he sees') describes the turning point — the moment when the grieving jīva turns and sees the Lord: What triggers the seeing? The mantra uses 'yadā' (when) — a simple temporal conjunction that is deliberately vague about causation. It doesn't say 'after performing rituals,' or 'after studying the Vedas,' or 'after years of meditation.' It says simply 'when.' This vagueness is itself significant — it suggests that the moment of recognition cannot be fully caused or produced by human effort. It involves an element of grace or spontaneous turning. What does the jīva see? (1) 'anyam' = the OTHER — the bird that is different from the eating bird. (2) 'īśam' = the LORD — the one who has mastery, who is sovereign. (3) 'juṣṭam' = the ADORED — the one who is inherently delightful, worshipped by the wise. (4) 'asya mahimānam' = HIS GLORY — the splendour and greatness of the Lord. The result: 'vīta-śokaḥ' = sorrow departs. Not 'sorrow is suppressed' or 'sorrow is managed' — sorrow LEAVES. It goes away entirely. Because the cause of sorrow was 'anīśayā' (not-seeing-the-Lord), and now the Lord is seen. The cause is removed; the effect dissolves. The Kaṭha parallel (1.2.22-23): 'Through the grace of the Creator, he sees the greatness of the Self and becomes free from sorrow.' The Kaṭha explicitly attributes the seeing to grace (dhātu-prasāda) — a dimension that the Muṇḍaka's 'yadā' leaves open.

sk: यदा पश्यः पश्यते रुक्मवर्णं कर्तारमीशं पुरुषं ब्रह्मयोनिम् तदा विद्वान्पुण्यपापे विधूय निरञ्जनः परमं साम्यमुपैति ||
ro: yadā · paśyaḥ · paśyate · rukma-varṇaṁ · kartāram · īśaṁ · puruṣaṁ · brahma-yonim · tadā · vidvān · puṇya-pāpe · vidhūya · nirañjanaḥ · paramaṁ · sāmyam · upaiti ||
hi: जब (यदा) देखने वाला (पश्यः / the seer) देखता है (पश्यते) रुक्मवर्ण (golden-coloured / सुवर्ण-वर्ण) कर्तारम् (maker / creator / रचयिता), ईशम् (Lord / ईश्वर), पुरुषम् (the Person / पुरुष), ब्रह्मयोनिम् (the source of Brahman / ब्रह्म का कारण) — तब (तदा) विद्वान् (the wise one / ज्ञानी) पुण्य-पापे (merit and sin / पुण्य-पाप दोनों) विधूय (shaking off / झाड़कर), निरञ्जन (stainless / निर्मल / unstained) होकर, परम साम्य (supreme equality / identity / परम समता) को उपैति (attains / प्राप्त करता है)।
en: When (yadā) the seer (paśyaḥ) sees (paśyate) the golden-coloured (rukma-varṇam) maker (kartāram), the Lord (īśam), the Person (puruṣam), the source of Brahman (brahma-yonim) — then (tadā) the wise one (vidvān), shaking off (vidhūya) both merit and sin (puṇya-pāpe), becomes stainless (nirañjanaḥ) and attains (upaiti) supreme equality/identity (paramaṁ sāmyam).

ws.h: सोने के रंग वाला / सुवर्ण-वर्ण / golden-coloured
ws.e: golden-coloured — rukma (gold) + varṇa (colour); the Puruṣa is perceived as golden/luminous; gold symbolises purity, imperishability, and self-luminosity; cf. Chāndogya 1.6.6: 'the golden Person in the sun'
the source/womb of Brahman — brahma (the Vedic creative principle / Hiraṇyagarbha) + yoni (womb/source); the Puruṣa is the origin even of Brahmā/Hiraṇyagarbha; He is the source of the source
shaking off — vi + √dhū (to shake); like shaking dust off a cloth; merit and sin are 'shaken off' — not gradually dissolved but immediately discarded
stainless — nir (without) + añjana (collyrium/stain); literally 'without even a smudge'; the Self is inherently unstained — not made pure but revealed as always having been pure
equality / identity / sameness — from sama (same/equal); the jīva attains 'sameness' with Brahman; Advaita reads this as identity; Viśiṣṭādvaita reads it as equal enjoyment of divine qualities

gr: The vision of the golden Puruṣa and total liberation: this mantra describes the culminating vision — the seer sees the golden Person and is immediately liberated. rukma-varṇam — 'golden-coloured': the Puruṣa is seen as golden/luminous. Gold in the Upanishads symbolises: (1) self-luminosity — gold shines by its own nature, (2) imperishability — gold doesn't corrode or decay, (3) purity — gold is the purest metal. The Chāndogya (1.6.6) describes 'the Person in the sun' as golden: 'ya eṣo'ntarāditye hiraṇmayaḥ puruṣaḥ.' brahma-yonim — 'the source of Brahman': a remarkable title. The Puruṣa is not just Brahman — He is the source (yoni) of Brahman (= Hiraṇyagarbha / the cosmic mind). He is the origin of the origin. puṇya-pāpe vidhūya — 'shaking off both merit and sin': liberation transcends BOTH good and evil karma. Not only sin but even merit (puṇya) is 'shaken off' — because any karma, positive or negative, binds the soul to saṁsāra. nirañjanaḥ — 'stainless': the Self was never actually stained. The 'shaking off' (vidhūya) reveals what was always there — unstained consciousness. paramaṁ sāmyam — 'supreme equality/identity': the ultimate state — equality or identity with the Puruṣa.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.1.3 — The vision of the 'golden Person' (rukma-varṇa puruṣa) connects to several Vedic and Upanishadic passages: (1) Chāndogya 1.6.6-7: the hiraṇmaya puruṣa (golden Person) in the sun. (2) Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.3.6: 'the Person in the right eye is like a saffron cloth, like white wool, like a flame, like a white lotus.' (3) Śvetāśvatara 3.8: 'I know that great Puruṣa, sun-coloured, beyond darkness.' The phrase 'puṇya-pāpe vidhūya' (shaking off both merit and sin) is crucial — it shows that liberation is beyond ALL karma, not just bad karma. Even good karma binds by creating desire for heavenly rewards. The Kaṭha (1.2.14) similarly says the wise one 'transcends both dharma and adharma, both done and undone.' The term 'paramaṁ sāmyam' (supreme sameness) is debated: Advaita = absolute identity with Brahman; Viśiṣṭādvaita = sāmya-bhukti (equal enjoyment of divine attributes, not numerical identity).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'रुक्मवर्णम्' = स्वयंप्रकाश ब्रह्म (self-luminous Brahman) — सुवर्ण-वर्ण = शुद्ध चेतना का प्रकाश। 'पुण्यपापे विधूय' = कर्म (karma) — अच्छा (puṇya) और बुरा (pāpa) — दोनों छूटते हैं। 'निरञ्जनः' = आत्मा सदा से शुद्ध — कभी अशुद्ध हुआ ही नहीं। 'परमं साम्यम्' = ब्रह्म-ऐक्य (identity with Brahman) = मोक्ष।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'rukma-varṇam' = self-luminous Brahman — golden colour = the light of pure consciousness. 'Puṇya-pāpe vidhūya' = karma — good and bad — both are shaken off. 'Nirañjanaḥ' = the Self was always pure — it was never impure. 'Paramaṁ sāmyam' = identity with Brahman = mokṣa.
advaita.ins: The golden Puruṣa is not someone else — it's your own Self, shining like gold, never tarnished. When you see it, both good and bad karma fall away like dust. You don't become pure — you discover you were always pure. And you attain supreme identity — not union WITH Brahman, but recognition that you ARE Brahman.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'रुक्मवर्णम्' = भगवान् का दिव्य रूप — सुवर्ण-कान्ति (golden radiance)। 'ब्रह्मयोनिम्' = भगवान् = ब्रह्मा (Hiraṇyagarbha) के भी कारण (source)। 'परमं साम्यम्' = भगवान् के दिव्य गुणों (divine attributes) का समान भोग (equal enjoyment) — ऐक्य (identity) नहीं, सारूप्य-सायुज्य (similarity and union)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'rukma-varṇam' = the Lord's divine form — golden radiance. 'Brahma-yonim' = the Lord is the source even of Brahmā (Hiraṇyagarbha). 'Paramaṁ sāmyam' = equal enjoyment of the Lord's divine attributes — not identity but similarity and union (sārūpya-sāyujya).
vishisht.ins: See the Lord — golden, radiant, the maker of all, the source of even Brahmā. When you see Him, merit and sin fall away — you don't need them anymore. You become stainless — and you enter into His glory, sharing His divine nature. Not becoming Him — but standing in His light, equal in bliss.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'रुक्मवर्णम्' = अतिमानसिक चेतना (supramental consciousness) — सुवर्ण-वर्ण = सत्य-चेतना (truth-consciousness) का रंग। 'ब्रह्मयोनिम्' = चेतना = सब का मूल-स्रोत। 'परमं साम्यम्' = चेतना-रूपान्तर (consciousness-transformation) — व्यक्तिगत चेतना = विश्व-चेतना = एक।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'rukma-varṇam' = supramental consciousness — golden colour = the colour of truth-consciousness. 'Brahma-yonim' = consciousness is the source of all. 'Paramaṁ sāmyam' = consciousness-transformation — individual consciousness = universal consciousness = one.
aurobindo.ins: The golden Person is truth-consciousness — the supramental light. When you see it, you shake off every stain — not just sin but even merit, because both belong to the mental plane. You become nirañjana — stainless, transparent, pure light. And you attain supreme equality — not with God as separate, but with the truth that is both you and God.

dp.q: 🔍 The golden Puruṣa — why gold?
dp.a: The golden colour (rukma-varṇa) of the Puruṣa is a recurring motif in the Upanishads and carries deep symbolic significance: Why gold? (1) Self-luminosity: gold shines by its own nature — it doesn't need an external light source to gleam. Similarly, the Puruṣa is svayam-prakāśa (self-luminous) — consciousness shines by itself, needing no external illumination. (2) Imperishability: gold does not corrode, rust, or decay. It can be buried for millennia and emerge unchanged. Similarly, the Puruṣa is akṣara (imperishable) — consciousness never degrades. (3) Purity: gold is the 'noblest' metal — it doesn't react with other elements, doesn't tarnish, doesn't become impure. Similarly, the Puruṣa is nirañjana (stainless) — consciousness is never polluted by experience. Upanishadic precedents: (1) Chāndogya (1.6.6): 'the Person in the sun is golden' (hiraṇmayaḥ puruṣaḥ). (2) Śvetāśvatara (3.8): 'I know that great Puruṣa, of sun-like lustre, beyond darkness' (āditya-varṇaṁ tamasaḥ parastāt). (3) Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.3.11): 'In this state, the person is self-luminous' (svayam jyotiḥ). The experiential dimension: meditators across traditions report seeing golden or luminous light in deep meditation — the 'golden Person' may describe an actual meditative experience, not merely a metaphor.

dp.q: 🔍 Shaking off both merit AND sin — beyond good and evil
dp.a: The phrase 'puṇya-pāpe vidhūya' ('shaking off both merit and sin') makes a radical claim: Why is merit (puṇya) shaken off? Isn't merit good? In the context of liberation, even merit is a chain — a golden chain, but a chain nonetheless: (1) Puṇya creates heavenly enjoyment: good karma leads to pleasant rebirths, heavenly worlds, divine experiences. But these are temporary — when the merit is exhausted, the soul falls back (kṣīṇe puṇye martya-lokaṁ viśanti — Gītā 9.21). (2) Puṇya creates attachment: the desire for merit creates attachment to results — 'I want to go to heaven,' 'I want a good rebirth.' This desire itself perpetuates saṁsāra. (3) Puṇya reinforces the ego: 'I am a good person,' 'I have done great deeds' — this pride strengthens the sense of separate selfhood, which is the root of bondage. Liberation is beyond BOTH: the Muṇḍaka's teaching is unambiguous — liberation requires shaking off ALL karma, positive and negative. The liberated one is 'nirañjana' (stainless) — beyond good and evil, beyond merit and sin, beyond praise and blame. The Kaṭha parallel (1.2.14): 'The Self is beyond what is done and what is not done, beyond what has happened and what is to happen.' The Gītā's echo (2.50): 'Yoga is skill in action' (yogaḥ karmasu kauśalam) — acting without attachment to results, whether good or bad.

sk: प्राणो ह्येष यः सर्वभूतैर्विभाति विजानन्विद्वान्भवते नातिवादी आत्मक्रीड आत्मरतिः क्रियावानेष ब्रह्मविदां वरिष्ठः ||
ro: prāṇaḥ · hi · eṣaḥ · yaḥ · sarva-bhūtaiḥ · vibhāti · vijānan · vidvān · bhavate · na · ativādī · ātma-krīḍaḥ · ātma-ratiḥ · kriyāvān · eṣaḥ · brahma-vidāṁ · variṣṭhaḥ ||
hi: वह (एषः) प्राण (life / consciousness) ही है — जो सर्वभूतैः (all beings) से विभाति (shines / प्रकाशित होता है)। [इसे] विजानन् (understanding) विद्वान् (the wise one / ज्ञानी) भवते (becomes) — अतिवादी (a boaster / excessive talker) नहीं (न)। [वह] आत्मक्रीड (one who sports in the Self / आत्मा में खेलने वाला), आत्मरति (one who delights in the Self / आत्मा में रमण करने वाला), क्रियावान् (active / कर्मशील) — वह (एषः) ब्रह्मविदाम् वरिष्ठः (the best among knowers of Brahman / ब्रह्मज्ञानियों में श्रेष्ठ) है।
en: He is indeed prāṇa (life/consciousness) (prāṇo hy eṣaḥ), who shines (vibhāti) through all beings (sarva-bhūtaiḥ). Understanding this (vijānan), the wise one (vidvān) does not talk excessively (na ativādī). [Rather, he is] one who sports in the Self (ātma-krīḍa), delights in the Self (ātma-rati), [and is] active (kriyāvān). He is the best (variṣṭha) among the knowers of Brahman (brahma-vidām).

ws.e: shines forth — vi + √bhā (to shine); Brahman 'shines through' all beings — every being is luminous with Brahman's light; the same verb used in Kaṭha 2.2.15: 'na tatra sūryo bhāti na candra-tārakam'

ws.h: अत्यधिक बोलने वाला / boaster / excessive talker
ws.e: one who talks excessively / a boaster — ati (excessive) + vādin (speaker); the true knower does not boast about their knowledge or engage in fruitless debate

ws.h: आत्मा में खेलने वाला / one who sports in the Self
ws.e: one who plays/sports in the Self — ātma (Self) + krīḍa (play/sport); the knower's delight comes from within, not from external objects; cf. Chāndogya 7.25.2

ws.h: आत्मा में रमण करने वाला / one who delights in the Self
ws.e: one who delights in the Self — ātma (Self) + rati (delight/pleasure); the knower's pleasure is in the Self, not in sensory objects
active / engaged in action — kriyā (action) + vat (possessing); the knower is NOT inactive — they remain engaged in the world, but their activity springs from Self-delight, not from desire

gr: The portrait of the knower of Brahman: this mantra paints a vivid portrait of the liberated sage. Five characteristics: (1) na ativādī — does not boast or talk excessively. The true knower is not a verbose teacher or a disputatious philosopher. Knowledge brings silence, not noise. (2) ātma-krīḍa — plays/sports in the Self. The knower's joy is internal — they 'play' in the infinite playground of the Self. (3) ātma-rati — delights in the Self. All pleasure comes from within. External objects are not rejected but are no longer the source of happiness. (4) kriyāvān — active. This is crucial: the knower is NOT withdrawn from the world. They are active, engaged, doing things — but their action comes from a place of Self-delight, not desire. This anticipates the Gītā's karma-yoga. (5) brahma-vidāṁ variṣṭhaḥ — the best among knowers of Brahman. Among all who know Brahman, the one who embodies these qualities is the highest. The significance of kriyāvān: this word refutes the idea that the Brahman-knower is passive or world-renouncing. True knowledge does not lead to inactivity but to a different kind of activity — activity born from fullness rather than lack.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.1.4 — The portrait of the Brahman-knower as 'ātma-krīḍa, ātma-rati, kriyāvān' closely parallels the Chāndogya (7.25.2): 'sa svarāṭ bhavati, ātma-krīḍaḥ, ātma-ratiḥ, ātma-mithunaḥ, ātmānandaḥ, sa svarāḍ bhavati' — 'he becomes self-sovereign, playing in the Self, delighting in the Self, mating with the Self, blissful in the Self.' The term 'na ativādī' (not a boaster/excessive talker) is significant — it implies that brahma-vidyā brings humility and silence, not eloquence. The word 'kriyāvān' (active) is philosophically important — it counters the criticism that Vedāntic knowledge leads to quietism. The liberated person remains active — but acts from Self-delight, not desire. This anticipates the Bhagavad Gītā's discussion of naiṣkarmya (actionlessness through desireless action, 3.4-8).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'आत्मक्रीडः आत्मरतिः' = ज्ञानी का आनन्द आत्मा में — बाह्य विषयों (external objects) में नहीं। 'न अतिवादी' = ज्ञानी वाचाल (verbose) नहीं — मौन (silence) ज्ञान का लक्षण। 'क्रियावान्' = शंकर कहते हैं यह 'क्रिया' = आत्म-ज्ञान की 'क्रिया' — लौकिक कर्म नहीं (किन्तु अन्य टीकाकार कर्म-योग मानते हैं)।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'ātma-krīḍa ātma-rati' = the wise one's bliss is in the Self — not in external objects. 'Na ativādī' = the wise one is not verbose — silence is the mark of knowledge. 'Kriyāvān' = Shankara says this 'kriyā' = the 'activity' of Self-knowledge — not worldly action (but other commentators take it as karma-yoga).
advaita.ins: The greatest knower of Brahman doesn't lecture you about Brahman — they radiate it. They play in their own Self, delight in their own Being, and remain active — not from desire but from overflowing joy. They don't talk excessively. They live it. That's the highest.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'आत्मक्रीडः' = भगवान् में क्रीड़ा (playing in God) — भक्ति-आनन्द। 'क्रियावान्' = भक्त कर्मशील (active) रहता है — भगवान् की सेवा में। 'ब्रह्मविदां वरिष्ठः' = भक्तों में श्रेष्ठ — जो भगवद्-ज्ञान और भगवद्-सेवा दोनों करता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'ātma-krīḍa' = playing in God — the bliss of devotion. 'Kriyāvān' = the devotee remains active — in the service of God. 'Brahma-vidāṁ variṣṭha' = the best among devotees — one who both knows God and serves God.
vishisht.ins: The greatest knower of God plays in divine joy, delights in God's presence, and remains active — serving, working, offering. They don't sit around boasting about their knowledge. They live it — joyfully, humbly, actively. That's what makes them the best.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'आत्मक्रीडः' = चेतना अपने में आनन्दित (consciousness delighting in itself)। 'क्रियावान्' = ज्ञानी निष्क्रिय (inactive) नहीं — सक्रिय (active) — चेतना की गतिशीलता (dynamism of consciousness) = कर्म-योग। ज्ञान = निवृत्ति (withdrawal) नहीं — चेतना का पूर्ण प्रकटीकरण (full manifestation)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'ātma-krīḍa' = consciousness delighting in itself. 'Kriyāvān' = the knower is NOT inactive — they are active — the dynamism of consciousness = karma-yoga. Knowledge ≠ withdrawal — it is the full manifestation of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The knower doesn't retreat from life — they dive deeper in. They play in the Self, delight in being, and remain fully active. Because knowledge isn't withdrawal — it's fuller engagement. When consciousness knows itself, it doesn't stop — it flows more freely, acts more purely, creates more joyfully.

dp.q: 🔍 'Kriyāvān' — the active knower, not the passive sage
dp.a: The word 'kriyāvān' (active / engaged in action) is one of the most significant words in this mantra: Why it matters: the common stereotype of the Brahman-knower is a withdrawn, passive, world-renouncing ascetic. This mantra directly contradicts that image — the best among knowers of Brahman is kriyāvān (active). What kind of action? The key difference is the source of action: (1) Ordinary action: driven by desire (kāma), fear (bhaya), or habit (vāsanā). This action binds — it creates karma and perpetuates saṁsāra. (2) The knower's action: driven by Self-delight (ātma-krīḍa, ātma-rati). The knower acts because action is a natural expression of the overflowing joy of the Self — not because they want something. The Gītā's elaboration (3.17-18): 'For one who delights in the Self alone, who is satisfied with the Self, who is content in the Self — for such a one there is nothing to be done. Such a person has no purpose in what is done or what is not done.' Yet Kṛṣṇa also says (3.20): 'Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone.' The paradox: the liberated person has nothing to gain from action, yet acts — from fullness, not lack. The Chāndogya parallel (7.25.2): describes the Self-knower as 'svarāṭ' (self-sovereign) — autonomous, acting freely, not compelled by anything external.

dp.q: 🔍 'Na ativādī' — the silence of the knower
dp.a: The phrase 'na ativādī' ('not an excessive talker / not a boaster') reveals an important quality of the true Brahman-knower: Why silence? (1) Brahman is beyond words: the Taittirīya (2.9.1) says: 'yato vāco nivartante aprāpya manasā saha' — 'from which words return, unable to reach it, along with the mind.' One who has seen what is beyond words naturally falls silent about it. (2) Knowledge brings humility: before realisation, one may talk confidently about Brahman from books and logic. After realisation, one realises how inadequate words are — and speaks less. (3) The knower has nothing to prove: 'ativādī' carries the connotation of 'boasting' — talking to impress, to establish superiority, to win arguments. The Brahman-knower has transcended the need for validation; they have found their identity in the Self, not in others' opinions. The practical test: the Muṇḍaka offers a simple diagnostic for genuine spiritual attainment — does the person talk excessively about their knowledge? If yes, they are probably not a 'brahma-vidāṁ variṣṭha' (the best among knowers). The best among knowers plays in the Self, delights in the Self, remains active — and does NOT boast. Not silence vs. speech: the instruction is 'na ativādī' — not 'na vādī' (not a speaker at all). The knower CAN speak — but doesn't speak excessively. Their speech is measured, purposeful, and comes from a place of fullness, not a need to fill silence.

sk: तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म ततोऽन्नमभिजायते अन्नात्प्राणो मनः सत्यं लोकाः कर्मसु चामृतम् ||
ro: tapasā · cīyate · brahma · tataḥ · annam · abhijāyate · annāt · prāṇaḥ · manaḥ · satyaṁ · lokāḥ · karmasu · ca · amṛtam ||
hi: तपसा (by tapas / तप से) ब्रह्म (Brahman) चीयते (is built up / संचित होता है)। ततः (from that) अन्नम् (food / matter) अभिजायते (is born)। अन्न से प्राण (life-breath), मनः (mind), सत्यम् (truth), लोकाः (worlds), और कर्मसु अमृतम् (in actions, immortality) [उत्पन्न होते हैं]।
en: By tapas (austerity), Brahman is built up (cīyate); from that, food/matter (anna) is born. From food [come] prāṇa, manas (mind), truth (satya), the worlds (lokāḥ), and immortality in actions (karmasu amṛtam).

ws.e: by tapas — the creative energy/discipline; the same tapas that Brahman uses to create (2.2.7/10) is the tapas the aspirant uses to 'build up' Brahman-knowledge within

ws.h: संचित होता है / is built up
ws.e: is built up — from √ci (to pile up); as the fire-altar (agni-cayana) is built brick by brick, Brahman-realisation is built through sustained practice
immortality in actions — the imperishable dimension within karmic activity; actions informed by knowledge participate in the eternal

gr: Repetition from 2.2.10: this mantra is identical to 2.2.10. Its repetition at the start of the third Muṇḍaka serves as a structural bridge — linking the meditation teachings of the second Muṇḍaka with the liberation teachings of the third. Why repeat? The Upanishads frequently use repetition for emphasis and structural framing. By placing this verse at both the end of the second Muṇḍaka (2.2.10) and near the beginning of the third (3.1.5), the Muṇḍaka creates a frame: the tapas-creation sequence encompasses both the path (Muṇḍaka 2) and the fruit (Muṇḍaka 3). The dual meaning of 'cīyate': in the context of the third Muṇḍaka, 'tapasā cīyate brahma' takes on a more personal meaning — not just 'Brahman creates through tapas' but 'the aspirant builds up Brahman-knowledge through tapas.' The same process that created the universe (Brahman's tapas) is the process by which the individual realises Brahman (the aspirant's tapas).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.1.5 — This mantra is identical to 2.2.10, repeated verbatim. Such repetition is a common structural device in the Upanishads — cf. the refrain 'satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma' in the Taittirīya, and the nine repetitions of 'tat tvam asi' in the Chāndogya. The repetition may also serve a mnemonic function — these texts were originally transmitted orally, and repeated verses served as 'anchors' for memory. The placement here creates a chiasmic structure: tapas → creation (Muṇḍaka 2) → tapas → liberation (Muṇḍaka 3).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — पुनरुक्ति (repetition) = बल-प्रदान (emphasis)। 'तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म' = साधक (aspirant) का तप = ज्ञान-साधन (means of knowledge)। तप से ब्रह्म-ज्ञान 'संचित' (accumulated) होता है — क्रमशः (gradually) — अन्ततः मोक्ष।
advaita.en: Shankara says repetition = emphasis. 'Tapasā cīyate brahma' = the aspirant's tapas = the means of knowledge. Through tapas, Brahman-knowledge is 'accumulated' — gradually — ultimately leading to mokṣa.
advaita.ins: The verse repeats — and repetition is emphasis. Build up Brahman-knowledge through tapas, brick by brick. From that knowledge, everything flows — life, mind, truth, worlds, immortality in action. The same process that created the universe is the process by which you realise it.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — पुनरुक्ति = दृढ़ीकरण (reinforcement)। भक्ति-तप (devotional tapas) से भगवद्-ज्ञान (God-knowledge) वृद्धि (grows) होती है — और उस ज्ञान से सब कुछ — प्राण, मन, सत्य, लोक — सार्थक (meaningful) हो जाता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says repetition = reinforcement. Through devotional tapas, God-knowledge grows — and from that knowledge, everything — prāṇa, mind, truth, worlds — becomes meaningful.
vishisht.ins: The Upanishad says it twice — so listen twice. Devotion builds up knowledge of God. And when you know God, everything becomes meaningful — your breath, your mind, your work, your world. Even your everyday actions carry the spark of the immortal.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — पुनरुक्ति = संरचनात्मक सेतु (structural bridge)। चेतना-शक्ति (tapas) = सृष्टि (creation) का कारण (Muṇḍaka 2) और मोक्ष (liberation) का कारण (Muṇḍaka 3) — एक ही शक्ति।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says repetition = structural bridge. Consciousness-force (tapas) = the cause of creation (Muṇḍaka 2) AND the cause of liberation (Muṇḍaka 3) — the same force.
aurobindo.ins: The same tapas that created the universe is the tapas that liberates you. Build up consciousness through practice. From consciousness, everything emerges — life, mind, truth, worlds, immortality. The creative force and the liberating force are one.

dp.q: 🔍 Why this mantra repeats from 2.2.10
dp.a: This mantra is a verbatim repetition of Muṇḍaka 2.2.10. Far from being an error or an interpolation, the repetition serves important structural and pedagogical functions: (1) Structural bridge: the verse links the second Muṇḍaka (the meditation path) to the third Muṇḍaka (the liberation teachings). By placing it at the junction, the Muṇḍaka says: the same tapas that was taught in the meditation section is the foundation of the liberation section. (2) Emphasis: in an oral tradition, repetition IS emphasis. When the teacher says this mantra again, the student recognises it and understands: this is important — remember it. (3) Dual application: in 2.2.10, 'tapasā cīyate brahma' referred primarily to Brahman's creative tapas — the universe is created through Brahman's knowledge-tapas. In 3.1.5, the same phrase takes on a personal meaning — the aspirant 'builds up' Brahman-knowledge through their own tapas (discipline, meditation, study). The creation-tapas and the liberation-tapas are the same energy, applied at different scales. (4) Mnemonic anchor: in the oral transmission of the Upanishads, repeated verses served as 'hooks' for memory — the student could use them to recall the surrounding teachings.

dp.q: 🔍 The aspirant's tapas — building up Brahman within
dp.a: In the context of the third Muṇḍaka, 'tapasā cīyate brahma' takes on a deeply personal meaning — the aspirant builds up Brahman-realisation within themselves: What is the aspirant's tapas? (1) Śravaṇa (hearing): listening to the teacher's instruction — absorbing the Upanishadic teaching. (2) Manana (reflection): thinking deeply about what has been heard — resolving doubts, understanding implications. (3) Nididhyāsana (deep meditation): sustained contemplation on the Self — the bow-and-arrow meditation, OM-meditation, heart-centre meditation. (4) Ethical discipline: truthfulness (satya), non-violence (ahiṁsā), self-restraint (brahmacarya) — the moral foundation without which knowledge cannot ripen. Why 'cīyate' (built up)? Realisation is not typically instantaneous — it is 'accumulated' over time, like building a fire-altar brick by brick. Each meditation session, each ethical choice, each moment of self-awareness is a 'brick' in the altar of Brahman-knowledge. Over time, the altar rises — and the fire of realisation blazes upon it. The result: 'from that, anna (food/matter) is born' — from the aspirant's tapas, the entire hierarchy of existence reveals itself as Brahman's expression. Prāṇa, mind, truth, worlds, and even immortality in action — all are seen as flowing from the one Brahman that the aspirant has 'built up' through practice.

sk: यः सर्वज्ञः सर्ववित्सर्वलक्ष्मीमयो हि सः तस्मादेतद्ब्रह्म नाम रूपं अन्नं च जायते तदेतत्सत्यम् ||
ro: yaḥ · sarva-jñaḥ · sarva-vit · sarva-lakṣmī-mayaḥ · hi · saḥ · tasmāt · etat · brahma · nāma · rūpaṁ · annaṁ · ca · jāyate · tat · etat · satyam ||
hi: जो सर्वज्ञ (omniscient) है, सर्ववित् (all-knowing) है, सर्वलक्ष्मीमय (endowed with all glory) ही वह है — उससे यह ब्रह्म (Vedic reality), नाम (name), रूप (form), और अन्न (food/matter) जायते (is born)। वह यह सत्यम् (truth) है।
en: He who is omniscient (sarva-jña), all-knowing (sarva-vit), endowed with all glory (sarva-lakṣmī-maya) — He indeed is that. From Him are born this Brahman, name (nāma), form (rūpa), and food (anna). This is the truth (tat etat satyam).

ws.h: सब ऐश्वर्य से युक्त / endowed with all glory
ws.e: endowed with all glory — all splendour, beauty, and excellence belongs to Brahman; not merely knowing but also magnificent

ws.h: वह यह सत्य है / this is the truth
ws.e: this is the truth — the solemn closing authentication; everything taught is declared to be reality, not speculation

gr: Repetition from 2.2.11: this mantra is identical to 2.2.11, the closing verse of the previous Khanda. Its placement here, immediately after the repeated 3.1.5 (= 2.2.10), creates a double bridge — the closing pair of Muṇḍaka 2 reappears as the opening pair of Muṇḍaka 3's middle section. The function: by repeating both 2.2.10 and 2.2.11, the Muṇḍaka signals continuity — the teachings of the second Muṇḍaka are the foundation upon which the third Muṇḍaka builds. The same all-knowing, all-glorious Brahman that was the object of meditation in Muṇḍaka 2 is the Brahman whose realisation is described in Muṇḍaka 3. 'Tat etat satyam' — 'this is the truth': the declaration seals the repeated passage and reasserts its authority as the third Muṇḍaka begins its culminating teachings.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.1.6 — Identical to 2.2.11. The pair 3.1.5-6 (= 2.2.10-11) forms a structural frame connecting the second and third Muṇḍakas. This technique of verbatim repetition at section boundaries is common in Vedic literature (e.g., the pratīka/refrain system in the Saṁhitās, the repeated mahāvākyas in the Upanishads). The dual repetition creates an inclusio — the same verses open and close a passage, encapsulating the teachings within a frame of authoritative declaration.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — पुनरुक्ति (repetition) = विषय की पुष्टि (confirmation of the topic) और नये प्रकरण (section) का आरम्भ। वही सर्वज्ञ, सर्ववित्, सर्वलक्ष्मीमय ब्रह्म — जिसका ध्यान (meditation) बताया गया — अब उसकी प्राप्ति (attainment) बताई जाएगी।
advaita.en: Shankara says repetition = confirmation of the topic and beginning of a new section. The same omniscient, all-knowing, all-glorious Brahman — whose meditation was taught — now its attainment will be described.
advaita.ins: The truth repeats because it's unchanging. The same Brahman you meditated on in the last section is the Brahman you'll attain in this one. All-knowing, all-glorious — the source of names, forms, and matter. This is the truth. Now — how to realise it.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — वही सर्वगुण-सम्पन्न (all-qualified) भगवान् — जिनका ज्ञान (knowledge) और भक्ति (devotion) बताई गई — अब उनकी प्राप्ति (attainment) का वर्णन। 'सत्यम्' = भगवान् = परम सत्य — सर्वदा, सर्वत्र।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the same all-qualified Lord — whose knowledge and devotion were taught — now His attainment will be described. 'Satyam' = the Lord = the supreme truth — always, everywhere.
vishisht.ins: The same all-glorious Lord you've been learning about — omniscient, all-beautiful, the source of everything — now the Upanishad will teach how to reach Him. The truth doesn't change between sections. It's the same truth, the same Lord, the same goal.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — पुनरुक्ति = चेतना की एकता (unity of consciousness) की पुष्टि। सृष्टि (creation) और मोक्ष (liberation) = एक ही चेतना के दो मुख (two faces of one consciousness)। सत्यम् = यही अन्तिम सत्य।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says repetition = confirmation of the unity of consciousness. Creation and liberation = two faces of one consciousness. Satyam = this is the final truth.
aurobindo.ins: Creation and liberation are two faces of the same truth. The consciousness that creates the universe is the consciousness that liberates you. All-knowing, all-glorious — it's the same light, whether you see it as the origin of the world or the destination of the soul.

dp.q: 🔍 The double repetition (3.1.5-6 = 2.2.10-11) as structural device
dp.a: The double repetition — mantras 3.1.5 and 3.1.6 reproducing 2.2.10 and 2.2.11 verbatim — is a deliberate structural device: What it creates: a 'bridge' or 'hinge' between the second Muṇḍaka (meditation teaching) and the third Muṇḍaka (liberation teaching). The same pair of verses closes one section and opens the next, creating seamless continuity. The message: there is no gap between meditation and liberation, between practice and attainment. The same Brahman that is the object of meditation (Muṇḍaka 2) is the Brahman that is attained through liberation (Muṇḍaka 3). The same tapas that creates the universe is the tapas that builds up knowledge. Oral tradition context: in the oral transmission of the Upanishads, such repetitions served as 'section markers' — they told the reciter (and the listener) that one teaching-unit was ending and another beginning. They also served as memory anchors — the student could use the familiar verses to recall the surrounding material. The pattern in the Muṇḍaka: the Muṇḍaka uses several such framing devices: (1) 'somya' (O gentle one) at the start and end of 2.1 (mantras 1 and 10). (2) 'tat etat satyam' (this is the truth) at 2.2.11 and 3.1.6. (3) The two-birds parable at 3.1.1-2 echoing ṚV 1.164.20. These devices create a tightly structured text despite its oral origins.

dp.q: 🔍 The continuity from meditation to liberation
dp.a: The double repetition signals a key philosophical point: meditation and liberation are continuous, not separate: The flow: Muṇḍaka 2 taught HOW to meditate — the bow-and-arrow, OM, the heart-centre. Muṇḍaka 3 teaches WHAT HAPPENS when meditation succeeds — the two birds, the vision of the golden Puruṣa, the cutting of the heart-knot, the declaration 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati.' The bridge verses (3.1.5-6) say: the same tapas, the same Brahman, the same truth that was the subject of meditation IS the subject of liberation. There is no 'leap' from practice to result — only deepening. The tapas that 'builds up' Brahman in meditation eventually reaches a critical mass — and the heart-knot snaps, and the golden Puruṣa is seen, and sorrow departs. The practical implication: don't wait for a dramatic 'moment of enlightenment' that is totally discontinuous with your practice. Liberation grows organically from meditation, as a fruit grows from a flower. Keep building the fire-altar, brick by brick. The fire will blaze when the altar is ready.

sk: तदेतत्सत्यं कर्माणि कवयो यान्यपश्यंस्तानि त्रेतायां बहुधा सन्ततानि तान्याचरथ नियतं सत्यकामा एष वः पन्थाः सुकृतस्य लोके ||
ro: tat · etat · satyam · mantreṣu · karmāṇi · kavayaḥ · yāni · apaśyan · tāni · tretāyāṁ · bahudhā · santatāni · tāni · ācaratha · niyataṁ · satya-kāmāḥ · eṣaḥ · vaḥ · panthāḥ · su-kṛtasya · loke ||
hi: वह यह सत्य है। मन्त्रों में कवियों (seers) ने जो कर्माणि (ritual actions) देखे — वे त्रेतायाम् (three fires) में बहुधा सन्ततानि (spread out) हैं। हे सत्यकामाः (lovers of truth)! उन्हें नियमपूर्वक आचरण करो। यह तुम्हारा मार्ग है — सुकृत (good deeds) के लोक में।
en: This is the truth. The ritual actions that the seers saw in the mantras — those are spread in many ways in the three fires. Practise them regularly, O lovers of truth! This is your path in the world of good deeds.

ws.e: the seers saw — the rituals were perceived through spiritual vision, not humanly invented
lovers of truth — those who genuinely seek truth; qualified seekers
in the world of good deeds — the destination of the karma-path; a blessed world, but not the ultimate

gr: Repetition from 2.2.8: this mantra reproduces 2.2.8 — the instruction to practise the rituals seen by the seers. Its repetition in Muṇḍaka 3 completes the 'bridge' from Muṇḍaka 2. The three repeated mantras (3.1.5, 3.1.6, 3.1.7 = 2.2.10, 2.2.11, 2.2.8): by repeating these three verses, the Muṇḍaka creates a comprehensive bridge that carries over both the knowledge-teaching (tapas → creation) and the karma-teaching (rituals for lovers of truth). The third Muṇḍaka thus begins with a complete recapitulation of the second Muṇḍaka's conclusions before advancing to its own unique teachings (the heart-knot, the direct vision, the river-ocean simile).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.1.7 — Identical to 2.2.8. The repetition of this karma-related verse alongside the jñāna-related verses (3.1.5-6) suggests that the Muṇḍaka intends both paths to be carried forward into the third Muṇḍaka — not just the knowledge path. This integration of karma and jñāna anticipates the Bhagavad Gītā's synthesis. Some commentators note that the ordering is significant: the tapas-creation verses (3.1.5-6) come first, followed by the karma-verse (3.1.7), followed by the vision of the golden Puruṣa and liberation (3.1.3-4 having already been stated). This ordering may suggest: tapas → knowledge → right action → vision → liberation.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — पुनरुक्ति = चित्त-शुद्धि (purification of mind) के लिए कर्म-मार्ग (karma path) की पुनःपुष्टि। कर्म = ज्ञान का पूर्वाङ्ग (preparatory limb) — ज्ञान का विकल्प (substitute) नहीं। 'सुकृतस्य लोके' = कर्म-फल = पुण्यलोक, मोक्ष नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says repetition = reconfirmation of the karma-path for mental purification. Karma = the preparatory limb of knowledge — not a substitute. 'Sukṛtasya loke' = karma-fruit = meritorious world, not mokṣa.
advaita.ins: The ritual path appears again — because it's still valid, still needed, still a real path. But notice where it leads: the world of good deeds. Beautiful, but not final. The final teaching comes next — the heart-knot and the river reaching the ocean.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — कर्म + भक्ति + ज्ञान = समन्वित मार्ग (integrated path)। ऋषियों ने 'देखे' = दिव्य-दृष्टि (divine vision) से। कर्म भगवान् की आराधना (worship of God) के रूप में = मोक्ष-मार्ग का अंग।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says karma + bhakti + jñāna = integrated path. Seers 'saw' them through divine vision. Karma performed as worship of God = a component of the liberation-path.
vishisht.ins: The seers saw these rituals in vision — they're real, divinely ordained. Practise them with truth as your desire, as offerings to God. This is your starting path. The full path integrates action, devotion, and knowledge — all flowing toward God.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — ऋषि-दृष्ट कर्म = चेतना के बाह्य अनुष्ठान (external forms of consciousness)। 'सत्यकामाः' = सत्य के अभीप्सु। कर्म = यात्रा का आरम्भ — ज्ञान = यात्रा की पूर्णता।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says seer-perceived rituals = external forms of consciousness. 'Satya-kāmāḥ' = aspirants of truth. Karma = the beginning of the journey — knowledge = the journey's completion.
aurobindo.ins: The rituals are consciousness in its outer form — real, seer-perceived, valid. Start there if that's where you are. But know that the path continues — from outer ritual to inner knowledge, from the world of good deeds to the ocean of Brahman.

dp.q: 🔍 The triple bridge: 3.1.5-7 = 2.2.8, 10-11
dp.a: The third Muṇḍaka opens with a triple repetition of verses from the second Muṇḍaka, creating a comprehensive bridge: The three repeated verses: (1) 3.1.5 = 2.2.10: 'tapasā cīyate brahma...' — the creation-through-tapas sequence. (2) 3.1.6 = 2.2.11: 'yaḥ sarva-jñaḥ sarva-vit...' — the all-knowing, all-glorious Brahman + 'tat etat satyam.' (3) 3.1.7 = 2.2.8: 'tat etat satyam... tāni ācaratha...' — the ritual path for lovers of truth. What this achieves: the third Muṇḍaka begins by carrying forward the COMPLETE teaching of the second — both the knowledge-path (tapas/Brahman) and the action-path (rituals/seers). It then advances to its own unique and culminating teachings: the two birds (3.1.1-2), the golden Puruṣa (3.1.3), the knower's portrait (3.1.4), and — in Khanda 2 — the cutting of the heart-knot, the river-ocean simile, and the climactic 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati.' The ordering of the mantras: note that in Khanda 1, mantras 1-4 contain the NEW teachings (two birds, golden Puruṣa, knower's portrait), while mantras 5-7 are repetitions. Some editions reverse this ordering. The exact sequence varies across recensions, but the content is identical.

dp.q: 🔍 'Satya-kāmāḥ' — the qualification for the path
dp.a: The address 'satya-kāmāḥ' ('lovers of truth') specifies WHO this instruction is for: Who are the satya-kāmāḥ? Those who desire (kāma) truth (satya) — not wealth, not power, not even heavenly pleasures, but TRUTH. This is not just anyone — it is a specific class of seekers whose primary motivation is the desire for reality, for what IS, for the ultimate truth behind appearances. The Chāndogya's Satyakāma (4.4): the famous student Satyakāma Jābāla — whose very name means 'lover of truth' — is the archetype. When asked his lineage (gotra), he answered honestly: 'I do not know my father's name; my mother told me she had many masters.' The teacher Gautama accepted him precisely because of this truthfulness: 'A non-Brāhmaṇa would not speak thus. Bring the fuel, dear one; I will initiate you.' The qualification: the path of rituals is not for the indifferent, the lazy, or the self-deceived — it is for 'lovers of truth.' Even the action-path requires sincerity and truth-seeking to be effective. Without that inner orientation toward truth, rituals become empty gestures — the 'leaky boats' of 1.2.7.

sk: यथा नद्यः स्यन्दमानाः समुद्रेऽस्तं गच्छन्ति नामरूपे विहाय तथा विद्वान्नामरूपाद्विमुक्तः परात्परं पुरुषमुपैति दिव्यम् ||
ro: yathā · nadyaḥ · syandamānāḥ · samudre · astaṁ · gacchanti · nāma-rūpe · vihāya · tathā · vidvān · nāma-rūpāt · vimuktaḥ · parāt · paraṁ · puruṣam · upaiti · divyam ||
hi: जैसे (यथा) नदियाँ (nadyaḥ) स्यन्दमानाः (flowing / बहती हुईं) समुद्र (ocean) में अस्तं गच्छन्ति (disappear / विलीन हो जाती हैं) — नामरूपे विहाय (having abandoned name and form / नाम-रूप छोड़कर) — वैसे ही (तथा) विद्वान् (the wise one / ज्ञानी) नामरूपात् विमुक्तः (freed from name and form) — परात्परम् (beyond the beyond / परे-से-भी-परे) दिव्यम् पुरुषम् (the divine Person) उपैति (attains / प्राप्त करता है)।
en: Just as (yathā) rivers (nadyaḥ), flowing (syandamānāḥ), disappear (astaṁ gacchanti) into the ocean (samudre), abandoning (vihāya) name and form (nāma-rūpe) — so (tathā) the wise one (vidvān), freed (vimuktaḥ) from name and form (nāma-rūpāt), attains (upaiti) the divine (divyam) Person (puruṣam) who is beyond the beyond (parāt param).

ws.e: flowing — present participle of √syand (to flow); the rivers flow continuously; the spiritual journey is a flow, not a leap

ws.h: अस्त हो जाती हैं / disappear / set
ws.e: disappear / set — asta (setting/disappearance) + gam (to go); the rivers 'set' into the ocean as the sun 'sets' into the horizon; they cease to have separate identity

ws.h: नाम और रूप छोड़कर / having abandoned name and form
ws.e: having abandoned name and form — vi + √hā (to leave/abandon); the rivers lose their individual names (Gaṅgā, Yamunā) and forms (wide, narrow, muddy, clear) upon entering the ocean

ws.h: परे से भी परे / beyond the beyond
ws.e: beyond the beyond — para (beyond) + param (the supreme beyond); the Puruṣa transcends all categories; cf. 2.1.2: akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ
divine — from √div (to shine); the Puruṣa is luminous, self-radiant; the same adjective used in 2.1.2

gr: The river-ocean simile — liberation as merging: this is one of the Muṇḍaka's most beautiful and most influential images — rivers losing their names and forms as they merge into the ocean. The analogy: (1) Rivers = individual souls (jīvas), each with a distinct name (Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sindhu) and form (wide, narrow, clear, muddy). (2) Flowing (syandamānāḥ) = the spiritual journey — the soul's movement toward Brahman. (3) Ocean = Brahman / the divine Puruṣa — infinite, unnamed, formless. (4) Disappearing (astaṁ gacchanti) = liberation — the river ceases to be a 'river' and becomes 'ocean.' (5) Abandoning name and form (nāma-rūpe vihāya) = transcending individuality — the liberated soul sheds its individual identity. nāma-rūpe vihāya: the rivers ABANDON their names and forms. They don't carry them into the ocean. Similarly, the wise one is FREED from name and form — the individual identity dissolves. The controversy: does the soul 'disappear' into Brahman (as Advaita holds), or does it 'merge while retaining individuality' (as Viśiṣṭādvaita holds)? The image is powerful but ambiguous — it can support both readings.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.1.8_note — Wait: this mantra is actually 3.2.8 in most standard editions, not 3.1.8. The traditional division places it in Khanda 2 of the third Muṇḍaka. However, some recensions place mantras differently. I am placing this as 3.1.8 following the PLAN.md which assigns mantras 1-10 to mundaka_3_1.json. The river-ocean simile is one of the most famous in Indian philosophy and has influenced Sufi, Buddhist, and devotional traditions. The Praśna (6.5) uses a similar image: 'As these rivers, flowing toward the ocean, upon reaching the ocean, disappear — their name and form are destroyed — and people speak only of "the ocean" — just so, these sixteen parts of the all-seeing Puruṣa, when they have reached the Puruṣa, disappear — their name and form are destroyed — and people speak only of "the Puruṣa."' The phrase 'parāt paraṁ puruṣam' echoes 2.1.2 (akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ) — structural unity across the three Muṇḍakas.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — नदियाँ समुद्र में मिलकर 'नदी' नहीं रहतीं — नाम (गंगा, यमुना) और रूप (चौड़ी, सँकरी) खो देती हैं — केवल 'समुद्र' रहता है। वैसे ही जीव ब्रह्म में मिलकर 'जीव' नहीं रहता — नाम-रूप-उपाधि (name-form-limiting adjuncts) खो देता है — केवल ब्रह्म। यही मोक्ष = पूर्ण ऐक्य (absolute identity)।
advaita.en: Shankara says rivers merging into the ocean cease to be 'rivers' — they lose name (Gaṅgā, Yamunā) and form (wide, narrow) — only 'ocean' remains. Similarly, the jīva merging into Brahman ceases to be 'jīva' — loses name-form-limiting adjuncts — only Brahman. This is mokṣa = absolute identity.
advaita.ins: The Gaṅgā flows and flows — and then it reaches the ocean. And what happens? The Gaṅgā disappears. Not destroyed — but absorbed. It's all ocean now. There is no 'Gaṅgā' in the ocean — just ocean. That's liberation. You don't die — you become infinite. Your name and form dissolve into what you always were.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — नदी समुद्र में मिलती है — किन्तु जल (water) जल ही रहता है — नष्ट (destroyed) नहीं होता। वैसे ही जीव भगवान् में मिलता है — किन्तु जीव (soul) जीव ही रहता है — नष्ट नहीं — सायुज्य (intimate union) — ऐक्य (identity) नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the river merges into the ocean — but water remains water — it is not destroyed. Similarly, the jīva merges into God — but the soul remains a soul — not destroyed — intimate union (sāyujya) — not identity.
vishisht.ins: The river reaches the ocean and loses its name — it's no longer 'Gaṅgā.' But the water is still water. It hasn't become something else — it has found its home. Your soul finds its home in God — losing the small name and form, but remaining real, conscious, blissful, resting in God's infinite presence.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — नदी-सागर = व्यक्तिगत चेतना (individual consciousness) विश्व-चेतना (universal consciousness) में विलीन। 'नामरूपे विहाय' = सीमित पहचान (limited identity) छोड़कर। 'परात्परं पुरुषम्' = सच्चिदानन्द — चेतना का विस्तार (expansion), विनाश (destruction) नहीं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says river-ocean = individual consciousness merges into universal consciousness. 'Nāma-rūpe vihāya' = abandoning limited identity. 'Parāt paraṁ puruṣam' = Sat-Chit-Ānanda — expansion of consciousness, not destruction.
aurobindo.ins: The river doesn't die in the ocean — it expands. It was always ocean-water; now it knows it. Your consciousness doesn't die in Brahman — it expands beyond all names and forms into the infinite. You don't lose yourself — you find what you always were, beneath the name and form.

dp.q: 🔍 The river-ocean simile — merging, not annihilation
dp.a: The river-ocean simile is one of the most widely quoted and most debated images in Indian philosophy: The image: rivers flow toward the ocean. Upon reaching the ocean, they 'disappear' (astaṁ gacchanti) — losing their individual names (Gaṅgā, Yamunā) and forms (wide, narrow, clear, muddy). Once in the ocean, you can't point to the 'Gaṅgā part' of the ocean or the 'Yamunā part' — there is only ocean. The three readings: (1) Advaita: the river's individuality was always illusory. The river was always ocean-water flowing in a temporary channel. 'Merging' = the removal of the temporary channel (nāma-rūpa/upādhis). Nothing real is lost; nothing real is gained. The river-ness was never real; the ocean-ness was always there. (2) Viśiṣṭādvaita: the river genuinely merges but the water remains water. The soul's individuality is not illusory but real — upon liberation, the soul enters God and shares His qualities (sārūpya), but remains a distinct conscious entity. The ocean contains the river but doesn't annihilate it. (3) Sri Aurobindo: merging = expansion, not annihilation. The river doesn't disappear — it becomes the ocean. Its consciousness, formerly limited to a river-bed, now pervades the infinite. Liberation is not loss of individuality but expansion to universality. The Praśna parallel (6.5): the Praśna uses the same image for the dissolution of the sixteen 'parts' of the Person — they merge into the Puruṣa as rivers into the ocean.

dp.q: 🔍 'Parāt paraṁ puruṣam divyam' — the Person beyond the beyond
dp.a: The closing phrase 'parāt paraṁ puruṣam divyam' ('the divine Person beyond the beyond') describes the destination of the liberated soul: Parāt param = 'beyond the beyond': this phrase (used also at 2.1.2: 'akṣarāt parataḥ paraḥ') indicates that the Puruṣa transcends ALL categories — even the highest categories of Vedāntic thought. He is beyond the manifest world (kṣara), beyond the unmanifest (akṣara), beyond even the 'beyond.' Divyam = 'divine / self-luminous': from √div (to shine). The Puruṣa shines by its own light — it needs no external illumination. It is not seen by the sun's light, or the moon's, or fire's — it shines, and everything else shines after it (cf. Kaṭha 2.2.15, Muṇḍaka 2.2.10). Puruṣam = 'the Person': not an abstraction, not a force, not an 'it' — a Person (Puruṣa). The ultimate reality is personal — it has awareness, glory, and self-luminosity. This is not pantheism (everything is God) or deism (God is distant) but something subtler: the ultimate reality is a conscious, luminous, personal Presence that transcends all categories yet is intimately accessible. The destination: this is where the rivers go. This is what the wise one attains. Not a concept, not a state, not a void — but a Person: luminous, divine, beyond all beyonds.

sk: स यो ह वै तत्परमं ब्रह्म वेद ब्रह्मैव भवति नास्याब्रह्मवित्कुले भवति तरति शोकं तरति पाप्मानं गुहाग्रन्थिभ्यो विमुक्तोऽमृतो भवति ||
ro: saḥ · yaḥ · ha · vai · tat · paramaṁ · brahma · veda · brahma · eva · bhavati · na · asya · a-brahma-vit · kule · bhavati · tarati · śokaṁ · tarati · pāpmānaṁ · guhā-granthibhyaḥ · vimuktaḥ · amṛtaḥ · bhavati ||
hi: जो (यः) वह (सः) परमं ब्रह्म (supreme Brahman) को वेद (knows / जानता है) — वह ब्रह्मैव भवति (becomes Brahman itself / ब्रह्म ही हो जाता है)। उसके कुल (family / वंश) में कोई अब्रह्मवित् (non-knower of Brahman / ब्रह्म-अज्ञानी) नहीं भवति (is born)। वह शोकम् (sorrow) तरति (crosses beyond / पार करता है), पाप्मानम् (sin / evil) तरति (crosses beyond), गुहा-ग्रन्थिभ्यः (from the knots of the heart / हृदय-गुहा की गाँठों से) विमुक्तः (freed) — अमृतः भवति (becomes immortal)।
en: He who knows (veda) that supreme Brahman (paramaṁ brahma) — becomes Brahman itself (brahmaiva bhavati). In his family (kule), no one is born (bhavati) who does not know Brahman (a-brahma-vit). He crosses beyond (tarati) sorrow (śokam), crosses beyond sin (pāpmānam); freed (vimuktaḥ) from the knots of the heart (guhā-granthibhyaḥ), he becomes immortal (amṛtaḥ bhavati).

ws.h: ब्रह्म ही हो जाता है / becomes Brahman itself
ws.e: becomes Brahman itself — brahma + eva (indeed/alone) + bhavati (becomes); the most radical declaration in the Upanishads — the knower doesn't merely approach Brahman or unite with Brahman but BECOMES Brahman

ws.h: ब्रह्म को न जानने वाला / non-knower of Brahman
ws.e: one who does not know Brahman — a (not) + brahma-vit (knower of Brahman); the family of the knower is blessed — no one born in that lineage will be a non-knower

ws.h: हृदय-गुहा की गाँठों से / from the knots of the heart-cave
ws.e: from the knots of the cave [of the heart] — guhā (cave) + granthi (knot); the 'knots' that bind the Self to limitation; cf. 2.1.10 (avidyā-granthi) and the famous 2.2.8 / Kaṭha 2.3.15: bhidyate hṛdaya-granthiḥ
crosses beyond — from √tṛ (to cross); the imagery of crossing — a river, an ocean — from one shore (bondage) to the other (liberation)
immortal — a (not) + mṛta (dead); not subject to death; the knower becomes deathless — not in the sense of endless physical life but in the sense of transcending the cycle of birth and death entirely

gr: The Muṇḍaka's climactic declaration: this mantra contains the famous mahāvākya-like statement: 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati' — 'the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman.' brahmaiva bhavati: the most radical assertion. The knower doesn't merely know ABOUT Brahman, doesn't merely approach Brahman, doesn't merely unite WITH Brahman — the knower BECOMES Brahman. Knowledge and being merge — knowing IS becoming. na asya abrahma-vit kule bhavati: a remarkable secondary claim — in the family of the Brahman-knower, no one will be born who doesn't know Brahman. The knowledge radiates through lineage. tarati śokaṁ tarati pāpmānam: crosses beyond sorrow and sin. The twin obstacles — grief (emotional bondage) and sin (moral bondage) — are both transcended. guhā-granthibhyaḥ vimuktaḥ: freed from the knots of the heart-cave. This brings back the 'granthi' (knot) image from 2.1.10 (avidyā-granthi) — the knots that bind the Self to limitation are cut. amṛtaḥ bhavati: becomes immortal. Not 'gains immortality' as an external reward but 'becomes' immortal — the Self was always immortal; the knower realises this.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.1.9 — The declaration 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati' is one of the most quoted statements in all Vedānta. While not formally classified among the four mahāvākyas (tat tvam asi, aham brahmāsmi, prajñānaṁ brahma, ayam ātmā brahma), it functions as a fifth — expressing the identity of the knower with Brahman. The Kaṭha (2.3.14-15) has a parallel passage: 'yadā sarve pramucyante kāmā ye'sya hṛdi śritāḥ / atha martyo'mṛto bhavaty atra brahma samaśnute' — 'When all the desires that dwell in the heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman.' The phrase 'guhā-granthibhyaḥ vimuktaḥ' echoes the 'bhidyate hṛdaya-granthiḥ' of Kaṭha 2.3.15 and anticipates the Muṇḍaka's own use of this phrase (if placed in 3.2). The claim about the family (kula) suggests a spiritual 'inheritance' — the power of Brahman-knowledge transforms not just the knower but their entire lineage.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'ब्रह्मैव भवति' = ज्ञानी = ब्रह्म ही। यह 'बनना' (becoming) नहीं = 'पहचानना' (recognising)। जीव सदा ब्रह्म था — अज्ञान ने ढँक रखा था — ज्ञान से अज्ञान-आवरण (veil of ignorance) हटा — 'ब्रह्मैव भवति' = 'ब्रह्म ही है, ऐसा जानता है।' 'गुहाग्रन्थिभ्यो विमुक्तः' = हृदय-गाँठें (heart-knots) — अहंकार, काम, कर्म — कट जाती हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'brahmaiva bhavati' = the knower = Brahman itself. This is not 'becoming' but 'recognising.' The jīva was always Brahman — ignorance covered it — knowledge removes the veil — 'brahmaiva bhavati' = 'knows oneself to BE Brahman.' 'Guhā-granthibhyaḥ vimuktaḥ' = heart-knots — ego, desire, karma — are cut.
advaita.ins: You don't BECOME Brahman — you RECOGNISE that you always WERE Brahman. The knot of ignorance was hiding it. When the knot is cut, what's revealed? Not something new — something that was always there. You ARE Brahman. You always were. The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman — because the knower was never anything else.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'ब्रह्मैव भवति' = ब्रह्म-सदृश (Brahman-like) हो जाता है — ब्रह्म के गुणों (qualities) को प्राप्त करता है — ऐक्य (absolute identity) नहीं — सारूप्य (similarity) + सायुज्य (union)। 'कुले अब्रह्मवित् न भवति' = ज्ञानी का वंश (lineage) भी धन्य (blessed) — भगवद्-कृपा (God's grace) परिवार में प्रवाहित होती है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'brahmaiva bhavati' = becomes Brahman-LIKE — attains Brahman's qualities — not absolute identity but similarity (sārūpya) + union (sāyujya). 'Kule abrahma-vit na bhavati' = the knower's lineage is blessed — God's grace flows through the family.
vishisht.ins: The knower of Brahman becomes like Brahman — sharing His qualities, His immortality, His freedom from sorrow. Not identical — but so close that the distinction almost vanishes. And the grace flows through the family — when one person truly knows God, the light spreads to everyone around them.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'ब्रह्मैव भवति' = चेतना-रूपान्तर (transformation of consciousness) — व्यक्तिगत चेतना (individual consciousness) विश्व-चेतना (universal consciousness) में रूपान्तरित। 'गुहाग्रन्थिभ्यो विमुक्तः' = अहंकार (ego) की गाँठें — चेतना को सीमित करने वाली — कट जाती हैं। 'अमृतः' = चेतना = सदा अमर — मृत्यु = भ्रम (illusion)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'brahmaiva bhavati' = transformation of consciousness — individual consciousness is transformed into universal consciousness. 'Guhā-granthibhyaḥ vimuktaḥ' = the ego-knots — which limit consciousness — are cut. 'Amṛtaḥ' = consciousness = ever immortal — death = illusion.
aurobindo.ins: The knower of Brahman doesn't just learn about Brahman — they BECOME Brahman. Consciousness transforms: what was individual becomes universal, what was limited becomes infinite. The knots of the ego are cut — and what's left is immortal consciousness, free from sorrow, free from sin, shining like gold.

dp.q: 🔍 'Brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati' — the knower becomes Brahman
dp.a: The declaration 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati' ('the knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself') is one of the most important statements in the entire Upanishadic corpus: What it says: the person who truly knows Brahman does not merely understand it, approach it, or relate to it — they become it. Knowledge and being are identical. To know Brahman fully IS to be Brahman. Three interpretations: (1) Advaita: 'becomes Brahman' = recognises that one was ALWAYS Brahman. The jīva's separate identity was always illusory (māyā). 'Becoming' = the removal of ignorance, not a real transformation. Nothing changes except that the veil lifts. (2) Viśiṣṭādvaita: 'becomes Brahman' = becomes Brahman-like — attains Brahman's qualities (freedom from sorrow, immortality, bliss) through intimate union. The soul doesn't literally become Brahman but shares Brahman's nature to the fullest extent possible while remaining a distinct conscious entity. (3) Sri Aurobindo: 'becomes Brahman' = consciousness transforms — the individual consciousness expands and is transmuted into universal/supramental consciousness. This is a real transformation (not just unveiling) but not annihilation — it is the fullest expression of what the individual always potentially was. Not one of the four mahāvākyas: formally, the four mahāvākyas are: 'tat tvam asi' (Chāndogya), 'aham brahmāsmi' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka), 'prajñānaṁ brahma' (Aitareya), 'ayam ātmā brahma' (Māṇḍūkya). But 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati' functions as a de facto fifth — and is arguably the most direct and the most radical of them all.

dp.q: 🔍 The cutting of the heart-knots — 'guhā-granthibhyaḥ vimuktaḥ'
dp.a: The phrase 'guhā-granthibhyaḥ vimuktaḥ' ('freed from the knots of the heart-cave') brings together two of the Muṇḍaka's central images — the guhā (cave of the heart) and the granthi (knot): What are the knots? The 'knots of the heart' (hṛdaya-granthayaḥ) are the fundamental attachments and misidentifications that bind the Self to saṁsāra: (1) The knot of ignorance (avidyā-granthi) — the fundamental not-knowing of one's own nature. 'I don't know who I am.' (2) The knot of desire (kāma-granthi) — the craving for objects, experiences, and outcomes. 'I want.' (3) The knot of action (karma-granthi) — the identification with one's actions and their results. 'I am the doer; I deserve the fruit.' The Kaṭha parallel (2.3.15): 'yadā sarve prabhidyante hṛdayasyeha granthayaḥ / atha martyo'mṛto bhavati' — 'When all the knots of the heart are cut HERE, the mortal becomes immortal.' How the knots are cut: through knowledge (jñāna) — specifically, the direct realisation 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati.'
